en: The Sūtra on the Illusionist Viśvantara, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

There were twelve hundred and fifty thousand followers and five thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were bodhisattvas possessed of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). All these great sages had attained *dhāraṇī* and unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Their names were:

Lion Bodhisattva, Lion-Mind Bodhisattva, Sincere-Delight Bodhisattva, Path-Ruler Bodhisattva, Great Ruler Bodhisattva, Radiant-Crown Bodhisattva, Radiant-Purity Bodhisattva, Tranquil-Mind Bodhisattva, Human-Brightness Bodhisattva, Enlightening-Humans Bodhisattva, Constant-Response Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī; along with sixty virtuous elders—all five thousand bodhisattvas—these were the leaders among them.
The Brahma King, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the various devas, as well as innumerable dragon kings and spirits, were present.
At that time, the king, ministers, elders, householders, and their retinues of officials provided the World-Honored One with offerings of clothing, food and drink, medicine, and bedding.
The World-Honored One’s fame is universally renowned and reaches afar;

he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

With the wisdom of all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he perceives everything universally without exception; he possesses the ten powers (*bala*) of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). He does not abandon great kindness (*maitrī*) nor relinquish great compassion (*karuṇā*); he is fully endowed with the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). His transformations are infinite: he attains the infinity of transformations through supernormal power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), transformations that explain the origins of things, and transformations that provide instruction.

In the mere instant of a thought, he can cause the great trichiliocosm—including its provinces, cities, rivers, and oceans; Mount Sumeru and its myriad mountains; the palaces of the nāgas, spirits, and devas; the Iron Ring Mountains, valleys, and streams; the ditches, pits, trees, and forests; and the kingdoms, towns, and villages—to be contained within a single pore for the duration of one kalpa, or even beyond another kalpa.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was an illusionist named Bhadra (translated into Chinese as Renxian, meaning "Benevolent and Virtuous"). He was well-versed in the scriptures and skilled in arts, possessing a profound understanding of illusory techniques. His work was ingenious and clever, bringing joy to many; his success was as he desired, and his fame spread far and wide. Among all other illusionists in the kingdom of Magadha, none could surpass him; wherever he went, he was the most eminent and foremost.
Except for those noble men and women who have seen the truths and attained the patience of the Dharma, there was not a single person among the populace who did not bow down in submission.
There was no one who was not deluded by what he said; following this unprecedented phenomenon, he obtained great offerings and sustenance through these illusory and heterodox practices.
When the illusory practitioner Renxian heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was renowned as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, he thought to himself:

"I have transformed the people of Magadha and all the cities and provinces, and there are none who do not receive my teaching; yet I alone have not yet converted the śramaṇa Gautama, nor have I ever tested him or his disciples."
"I should test whether they can be led astray;
if they can be led astray, the people of Magadha will all unite their hearts to come and serve me.
Thereupon, Renxian, relying on his original merit and sustained by the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.

Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose radiance surpassed that of the sun and moon by hundreds of thousands of billions of times—his light pure and stainless, its flames shining afar; his usnīṣa resplendent like a mani-jewel, brilliant as a lotus in its purity; and hearing him preach the Dharma with a voice surpassing that of the Brahmās and the eight classes of beings to deliver them extensively—he beheld the Buddha’s form-body, complete and exquisitely adorned. His heart leaped with joy, and he thought to himself:
"I wish to test the Buddha’s wisdom of all supernormal powers to see whether it truly perceives everything."
He then proceeded toward the Buddha, prostrated himself in salutation, and for the purpose of testing the Buddha, made this request:
"If he knows my intention, he will surely not accept the invitation; if he does not know it, he will certainly accept without doubt."
The Buddha, knowing his intention and out of compassion for Renxian and all the people of Rājagṛha, desiring to deliver them, silently accepted the invitation along with the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, Renxian thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses neither the various supernormal powers nor universal vision; since he lacks such insight, I shall now test him.
Thereupon, Renxian bowed his head in prostration, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The illusory man Renxian harbors deceit within his heart; he has invited the Buddha and the Sangha—how should we accept this?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

“Be silent for now; the Tathāgata has profoundly investigated how all beings have been deluded throughout the long night, and thus he establishes them through the practice of equanimity. Among the heavens and the world, there is none capable of defiling or deceiving the Buddha.”

The Tathāgata has severed lust, anger, delusion, and confusion; having extinguished all remaining defilements and eliminated every bond and attachment, he is free from the eighty impurities and has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Therefore, there is nothing within the triple world that can delude him; how could a minor illusory spirit possibly deceive him?

The Tathāgata has fully understood and mastered that all phenomena are like illusions; having attained supreme perfect enlightenment himself, he causes the realms of sentient beings and their very origins to all transcend through skillful illusion. No matter how virtuous or wise one may be, they can never equal the Buddha’s illusory arts—not even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or countless billions of times—and no metaphor can ever serve as a sufficient comparison.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "What do you think?
Is the illusory man Renxian able to adorn and transform a trichiliocosm so that it becomes pure and beautiful?"
He replied, "Indeed, this illusionist cannot do so.
The Buddha said:

"In the mere instant that the Tathāgata forms his intention, he can cause the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system to be purified and enter into a single pore; yet the Buddha’s illusory artifice is ultimately never delusive."
Even if there were winds named Sulāna and Chedana in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions that blow away and destroy the trichiliocosm, yet it would be restored to its former state;
there are winds named Anupatana and Sthitisthāpana that revolve throughout the world;
and there is a wind named Parittana that circulates through the thirty-two heavens.
There is a wind named "Crushing and Destroying Mount Sumeru";
there is a wind named "Kunala," which raises great fires that reach as high as the Thirty-two Heavens;
there is a wind named "Ever-Arising," which initiates the conflagration that consumes the world at the end of an eon.
There is a wind named Blazing Fire, which causes the trichiliocosm to burn all at once;
there is a wind named Pouring Rain, which raises great showers;
and there is a wind named Drying Up, which completely eliminates the calamity of floods.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"I have now briefly stated the names of these winds; from kalpa to kalpa, there is no end to them.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?"

Is there anyone who can arrest the void, sit amidst the various winds, perform the fourfold vessel-acts, and cause these winds to enter a single mustard seed, such that within the mustard seed there is no obstruction and no harm, allowing all devas and humans to dwell in peace and enjoy themselves without fear?
“The Tathāgata’s illusory dharmas further transcend this, being without limit; they are not within the reach of the stages of the disciples or the pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana stood before the assembly, prostrated himself in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!”
We have attained a sublime benefit.
Why is this? Because the majestic power of the World-Honored One is so lofty and vast, and his supreme dignity is thus boundless.

When the people heard of these miraculous transformations of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they leaped for joy at having attained such excellent benefit; they immediately resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and in that single moment, they were filled with immeasurable merit.

Thereupon, the illusory man Renxian entered the city of Rājagṛha and returned home. That very night, in the most foul and impure place within the city where filth accumulated, he manifested a great lecture hall. He hung silk streamers and flowered canopies, raised banners and pennants, and made the ground appear level and even. Trees grew lush and flourishing, while jars, precious vessels, incense burners, and lamps were scattered about, filled with various flowers and fragrances.

Beside the lecture hall, he planted eight thousand jewel trees whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were of manifold colors and fragrances; beneath each tree, he prepared lion seats for the bhikṣus.

In the center of the lecture hall, a lion throne was specially prepared for the Tathāgata; its legs were fashioned from various jewels and adorned with immeasurable splendor, standing four zhang and nine chi high.

On the four sides of his seat, he manifested four precious trees and prepared various kinds of food consisting of a hundred flavors; those who made these offerings numbered five hundred, their bodies adorned with precious necklaces, upright and radiant.
After the illusory man Renxian had thus manifested these things, the Four Heavenly Kings went to the illusory hall created by the illusory man and said to Renxian:
"Excellent, O worthy one!"

He then requested that the Tathāgata reside in this lecture hall and receive his offerings, saying, "May you permit me to assist with whatever is lacking; I wish to construct a palace to serve the Tathāgata."
Thereupon, Renxian (Bhadra) was even more filled with exultation at having attained what he had never experienced before, and replied:
"I shall listen,
O Heavenly King!"
"You should know that now is the time.
Thereupon, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately manifested a palace of exquisite and peerless beauty, such that the one built by Bhadrapāla was eclipsed and no longer visible.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with thirty-two thousand ladies-in-waiting, arrived at the lecture hall of the illusory practitioner and said to Bhadrapāla:
“Excellent! How wonderful!

You have truly attained a great benefit in inviting the Tathāgata to this Hall of Adorned Transformation to make offerings to the Buddha. Would you allow me to assist you with whatever you lack? I wish to construct a palace to serve as a residence for the Tathāgata.”
"Then, O Benevolent and Wise One!
You were all the more leaping with joy at what you had never experienced before, and you privately wondered in astonishment?
He replied:
“Listen, Śakra! You should know that now is the time.”

The Lord of Devas immediately manifested a great palace that surpassed the most excellent palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; he manifested and planted jewel trees that excelled the exquisite beauty of the Yaṣṭi and Kovidāra trees, eclipsing the lecture halls, palaces, and various adorned trees established by the Benevolent and Wise Ones and the Four Heavenly Kings.
The benevolent and wise one then thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One is no ordinary being; such divine and wondrous deities and sons of heaven as these are arising great offerings to serve the Tathāgata. Now, were I to destroy what I have established, it would be a great delusion. How could I bear to offer this to the Most Honorable One above?"

Thereupon, Renxian (Bhadra) wished to make his illusions vanish, yet he could not extinguish them; though he performed all manner of arts and spells, they could not be made to cease. The illusory food, the offerings, the decorations of the lecture hall, and the lion throne became eternally real and could no longer be changed.
Bhadrika was struck with wonder and thought to himself:

"What was previously said—that it would appear when manifested as an illusion and vanish when one wished for its disappearance—why is it that now, having been transformed by the Tathāgata into a magical offering, it cannot be changed?"
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what Bhadrika was thinking, addressed him, saying:

"Just as you have manifested these pure and adorned offerings for the Buddha, they cannot be transformed back into their original state; therefore, by beholding the Tathāgata, you shall give rise to a heart of joy, and you will always attain peace and security until you reach the path of Nirvāṇa."
At that time, Bhadrika was filled with joy and delight; in the early morning, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "The time for the meal has arrived; I pray that you will deign to come.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One—
Having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus, the Buddha proceeded to the Hall of Renxian Adornment.

At that time, the Buddha manifested a transformation such that Renxian perceived him seated upon a lion throne he had prepared; the Four Heavenly Kings likewise saw the Tathāgata seated upon a lion throne fashioned within the palace they had built.
Śakra thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata is sitting upon the seat of adornment manifested by me.
At that time, the various followers of heterodox paths in Rājagṛha who did not believe in the Dharma abandoned their arrogance and anger, and all together proceeded to the Hall of Adornments.
"Today we shall together witness the miraculous responses manifested by Gautama.
The men and women of that borderland who followed the pure Dharma all rejoiced and went together to the lecture hall, saying:
"Today we shall behold the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; we shall hear his lion’s roar and witness his transformations."
Thereupon, Renxian (Bhadra) cast off his arrogance, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“I only pray that the Tathāgata will forgive my transgressions. Out of my original folly, I sought to disturb the Tathāgata by magically creating this food to assist the attendants, as well as these lion thrones, all of which were likewise conjured.”
In his heart he felt remorse, wishing to extinguish and dissolve that which had been manifested through transformation.
The Buddha, as the Holy Honored One, regarded him with compassion and forgiveness, ensuring that all that had been performed would not be subject to further change.
Thereupon, the Buddha told Renxian:

"All people and all that they possess are like illusions and transformations; the bhikṣus seated here are also like illusions and transformations; even my own body is likewise an illusion of wisdom. This trichiliocosm is further a transformation, and all dharmas—whether arising from causes and conditions of sin or merit—are also like illusions and transformations, each occurring through the convergence of causes and conditions."
He then took the magically produced food and utensils and distributed them for their use.

Thereupon, the illusory man Renxian, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and all those who had assisted in the offering, held up the magically produced food and made offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the worthy Mahākāśyapa spoke these verses:
"The seats now prepared, and those who sit upon them—
With minds fixed in equanimity, well done is this unsurpassed giving."
Śāriputra spoke in verse:
“The mind with which one offers these requisites today, and the intention of the recipient;
if one always maintains such perfect awakening, one will swiftly bring this gift of faith to completion.”
Subhūti spoke in verse:
"In this giving, there is nothing given; the recipient has nothing received.
For one who acts in accordance with this, this is the perfection of the gift of faith."
Ānanda recited this verse:
“This giving is the supreme vehicle; the one who eats has no [discursive] mind.
With body and mind free from attachment, he is the benefactor of the world.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī said:
"Just as that illusory man, O Benevolent and Wise One, manifests this transformation;
so too it is with all worlds, yet the foolish do not understand it."
The Bodhisattva Guangzao said:
"For example, sitting beneath a tree, one perceives all things as created through illusion;
that which is illusory is also empty, being exactly equal and without distinction."
The Bodhisattva Siṃha said:
"When the lion's roar is not heard, small beasts cry out among the trees;
as soon as the lion lets forth his thunderous roar, they flee and scatter in the ten directions."
"Venerable and worthy one, you harbor resentment and delude the people with illusions;
yet the illusions manifested by the Tathāgata cannot be resisted by any of the māras.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Siṃhamati.
"This food is a transformation; those who provide the offerings are likewise illusory.
Those who eat the food are all transformations—excellent is this unsurpassed sacrifice.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
"As when oil and ghee are poured onto a fire, its brilliance becomes even more intense;
so too is the illusion of the Benevolent and Wise—one, the Buddha-illusion, manifests universally.
The youth Maitreya said:
"Just as this very place, for instance, is entirely a magical creation;
the illusions produced by the Benevolent and Wise deceive and delude the multitude.
All phenomena are likewise: fundamentally, they are all equal."
"Unaware of the future, you, a fool, wander through birth and death.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to convert the lay devotee Renxian, manifested a palace to the east of the lecture hall; the elder occupied its center and said to Renxian:
"What are you doing now?"
He replied, "I am making offerings to the śramaṇa Gautama and the community of bhikṣus.
The householder responded:
“O Māyāvin! Do not speak such words; the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus are now eating in the palace of King Ajātaśatru.
At that time, Renxian, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, saw the Buddha and the Saṃgha eating in the royal palace.
At that time, the Buddha again manifested as an elder who entered the lecture hall and asked Renxian,
"What are you doing now? He replied:
"I am now making an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The elder replied, "Do not speak such words; the Buddha and the Sangha are currently traveling along a different path for alms."
At that time, Renxian, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, saw the Buddha’s assembly begging for alms on a side road.
Furthermore, an elder approached Renxian and asked,
“What are you doing now?”
He replied, "To offer to the Buddha and the assembly. The elder replied:
"Do not say such words; the World-Honored One is currently in the rear garden of Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, expounding the Way of the Sūtras for the fourfold assembly.
By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power, Renxian beheld the Buddha in the rear garden of Jīvaka, preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Bhadrika, "What are you doing now? He replied:
"I shall provide offerings for the Buddha and the assembly.
Śakra replied, "Do not say such words;
at present, the Tathāgata is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, preaching the Dharma to the devas and humans beneath the Day-and-Night Tree."
Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the virtuous Renxian saw the Buddha in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma to devas and humans.

The illusory master Renxian also saw that upon every tree, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were all adorned with jeweled thrones; upon these transformed lion seats sat Tathāgatas, complete with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, surrounded by assemblies of monks.
The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā King all manifested lion thrones upon which they saw the Tathāgata seated;

likewise, throughout the streets, lanes, alleys, lodgings, and dwellings of Rājagṛha City, everyone saw the Tathāgata appearing before all the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, and everyone saw Renxian repenting his transgressions and commending himself.

At that time, what the benevolent and wise one saw with his eyes was nothing else but the Tathāgata. The illusory man leaped for joy and immediately gave rise to a virtuous mind; because of this gladness, he attained the Buddha-mind Samādhi. Rising from that meditative state, he joined his palms before the Buddha and questioned him in verse:
"Now I behold the supernatural power of the Tathāgata;
In the mere instant of forming a thought, he manifests many Buddhas."
Their number is in the hundreds of thousands, exceeding even this limit;
like the sands of the Ganges, such are the Buddhas.
Originally, I thought myself one who had extensively studied illusory arts;
In Jambudvīpa, there is none equal to him.
Beholding today the Buddha’s supernormal powers,
no calculation or analogy can serve as a comparison.
Now with my own eyes I behold nothing else;
I see everywhere all the Buddhas, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Therefore, I now wish to ask the Dharma King: where is this Buddha?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain:
which Buddha did you serve to receive the foremost offerings?
To which Buddha should one give so that the merit is greatest? What is purity?
O One who receives offerings, the Benefactor of the Multitudes!
We pray that you will explain this for us—the universal vision of equality.
We now confess our transgressions and all that we have committed.
One who has encountered a Buddha, a hero of the world and a guide,
yet fails to show reverence toward such a venerable person,
brings about their own ruin and shall not attain their aspirations.
The devas have already heard it, as has Śakra!
Thus, throughout this entire assembly, all have universally attained understanding.
I now give rise to the bodhicitta.
For the sake of all beings, I now deliver them all.
Now I make this request on behalf of all sentient beings:
may they all be fully satisfied with the nectar of immortality and abide in peace.
May those who are fast asleep quickly attain awakening;
may they reach the marvelous illumination of the lamp of wisdom.
Who is able to perform such transformations as these that are manifested?
Hearing what they say, one finds them stable and gentle;
their wisdom is unimpeded, and their practice is most supreme.
They give rise to no [discursive] mind, for their aspiration for the Way is most honored.
I pray that you will explain for me the practice of the subtle and wondrous Way;
by honoring which venerable one can one swiftly attain the path of the Buddha?
How is it that such a person is said to be fully endowed with the practice?
Beyond the reach of all disciples,
what kind of virtue is this practice of non-practice?
What is its true meaning?
Listen attentively to what is called "that which is cherished": the etiquette of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).
How does one give rise to it, so that no doubt arises?
What is diligence such that one never tires of hearing and receiving [the Dharma]?
When will one attain firmness in listening?
And how should one expound the teachings of the Dharma?
What is meant by radiance, such that all dharmas illuminate people?
How does one bestow the Way and attain compassionate conduct?
How does one establish a mind free from differentiation?
What is meant by making offerings so that they are fully provided wherever one goes, and how does one cultivate steadfast compassion toward all people?
What constitutes a true spiritual teacher?
One should respectfully practice and emulate them;
as for what constitutes an evil friend,
one should distance oneself from them.
How can one go to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
Having already attained the opportunity to meet him, how should one make offerings?
What training should one study to become most venerable?
How should one train diligently to attain wisdom?
And how, regarding the precepts, does one become pure?
How does one attain the concentrated mind of samādhi?
What is established to accomplish pure and solemn conduct?
How does one relinquish that which is contrary to the Dharma?
How does one subdue the mind while on the Path;
how does one manifest the subjugation of Māra and the fetters of sensual desire?
How does one listen to and receive the teachings, and contemplate the meaning of the sūtras?
How is it that his mind does not abandon any sentient beings?
How does he teach and transform the multitudes of people and creatures,
so that they firmly uphold virtue and have no place for [deluded] action?
How is it that one acts among people without abandoning them;
what are the traces of skillful means, compassion, and benevolent love?
How does one come to be fully endowed with supernormal powers?
What is meant by resolve, and what is the sublime distinction of the mind of the Way?
How does one bring all things to fulfillment according to one's vows;
how does one attain analytical discernment, the dhāraṇīs, and the patience of the Dharma?
With eloquence purified, one’s practice is non-retrogressive;
with profound meaning, one is foremost in understanding the significance.
How is it that herein one attains ultimate transcendence?
Having already attained the realization of the Way, you understand it with subtle clarity;
you know all things—this is the practice of the Buddha-way.
Firmly abiding in the Way, you do not waver or turn back.
I only pray that you will explain this most sublime meaning;
the wisdom of all supernormal powers, as brilliant and vast as the ocean.
O World-Honored One, out of compassion, I pray that you will speak it for me.
"I contemplate that I shall attain it and firmly practice it.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses for the illusory practitioner Bhadra:
"One who is able to understand and know That all phenomena are transformations;..."
They are able to manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas;
they can also manifest their arrival at hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-lands.
In every place they reach, they deliver hundreds of millions of sentient beings.
O benevolent and wise one!
Though devoid of form and color,
you are able to manifest forms, so that immeasurable numbers may behold them.
It has no arising, nor does it have cessation;
one does not see its coming, nor is there a place where it goes.
Thus it is, O worthy one!
That Buddha and the holy beings manifested the body of a Buddha, as well as a community of bhikṣus;
they came from nowhere, nor was any place of abiding seen.
Wisdom is inconceivable; this is the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Just as in a magical illusion, where causes and conditions are one and the same, there appear elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and people.
There is no one who sits, nor is there any place to which they go;
this is a matter of inversion, yet people call it correct.
All Buddhas are thus: they possess no physical body.
It has no form or image, nor does it act in any place.
Those who perceive their own bodies seek out its location;
those who awaken do not perceive it, having eliminated all conceptualizations.
The Buddha has no form or appearance, being free from the primary and secondary marks;
he does not arise from a lineage, and when contemplated, he is invisible.
He possesses neither sound nor speech.
Without mind, intellect, or consciousness, one is free from all recollection and thought.
As the Buddha has awakened to it, this is truly the way things have always been:
the three periods of time are entirely empty, and no conceptualization arises.
Always not giving rise to conceptual thought, one has already seen original purity;
therein no phenomena exist, for all their virtues are auspicious.
That which the Buddha brings forth is originally pure and beyond measure.
There are no four great elements, nor are there any aggregates or coverings.
That which they dwell in is unmoving and unattached;
yet they cannot clearly perceive it with the eye of wisdom.
As I have realized it, one attains the vision of the Buddha;
yet such a person has never before seen the World-Honored One.
To see that there is nothing to be seen is to behold the Teacher.
It is like raising one's hand to grasp at empty space;
so it is with the Buddhas you have seen, O virtuous and noble one!
All are of one meaning; they should be established in equanimity.
I am likewise, no different from other Buddhas;
all right wisdom is equal in its characteristic.
Their precepts are pure, and their samādhi is equanimous;
their concentration and wisdom, as well as their liberation, are equanimous.
Thus, through the equality of wisdom, they transcend the affairs of knowledge and vision.
All powers are the name and virtue of the Buddha.
The meaning of emptiness is equal, as are the traces of the path;
all dharmas abide therein without obstruction.
All things are like illusions, fundamentally pure and liberated;
there is nothing to be accomplished, yet that which arises is majestic and pure.
You, O Benevolent and Worthy One, should know that having made offerings to even one Buddha;
Having already served the Buddhas of the ten directions,
because the Dharma is thus equal, one may seek for various things, yet ultimately they cannot be found.
All can purify the faithful offerings of people;
all that is given results in great virtue.
All are pure, arising from the equality of dharmas.
The Buddha is neither manifold nor distinct;
all things are entirely and truly the Buddha!
Those who engage in inverted conduct do not see the Buddha.
Now, these manifested forms shown by all the Buddhas have entirely ceased;
they are equal and leave no trace behind. It is just as you, O virtuous and noble one!
Mindfully contemplate the Buddha you have seen!
Just as a skillful artisan creates a transformation-body, so too should you contemplate the five aggregates; it must be in this manner!
All that is attached to the various veils, as well as ignorance and folly—
these are non-arising, unreal, and non-existent;
in this state of non-existence, there is likewise nothing established.
This is invisible, and it has no form;
having observed this clearly, one cannot remain long.
The five aggregates are spontaneous and, in this regard, are like an illusion.
Sentient beings engage in strife and litigation, greedily clinging to the marks of their own bodies.
Yet these are but manifested marks of the markless;
thus, the Buddha-way of perfect awakening remains as distant as it ever was.
The dharma of falsehood is the locus from which manifold perceptions arise;
it generates various causes and conditions, a formless tree that produces all manner of phenomena through diverse types of mental activity.
To sever all sensations and perceptions is to realize primordial non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*).
One who understands dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as well as karmic formations—
that person comprehends the Dharma and attains freedom from desire.
"Having become detached from the phenomena of desire, one immediately recognizes suchness;
one immediately attains the vision of the Path, and one's eye becomes pure.
When the Buddha spoke this verse, the illusory man Renxian attained the patience of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti).
Five thousand people who had never before resolved their minds toward enlightenment all generated the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true awakening;
two hundred devas and humans became free from dust and defilement, and their Dharma-eye was purified.
Then, after the Buddha had finished eating the transformed food, wishing to augment the merit of the benevolent and worthy one’s gift of faith, he spoke these verses:
"Thus, without expectation of reward, that which is given attains purity;
with all requisites for giving complete, the virtue of the benevolent and worthy one is fulfilled."
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that, World-Honored One,
you cause this transformed lecture hall to remain for seven days and nights, so that it does not vanish."
The Buddha then, by means of his majestic spiritual power, caused the transformed lecture hall to remain standing for seven days and nights without perishing, its adornments remaining as they were.

At that time, the Buddha rose from his seat and, together with the bhikṣus, the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was to listen to and receive the Dharma.
Thereupon, Renxian went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and then stood with palms joined, addressing the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One!
“How many paths of practice and dwelling places must a bodhisattva possess in order to reach the site of enlightenment and clearly comprehend the true meaning?
Thereupon, the Buddha told Renxian:
“Listen attentively and reflect upon this well!”
"I shall now explain for you the bodhisattva’s place of awakening.
Thereupon, O Benevolent and Wise One!
together with the great assembly, they received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"There are four matters by which a bodhisattva abides in the Way and attains the site of enlightenment:
the first is that their mind constantly practices all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms."
Second, not abandoning any sentient being;
third, seeking merit without weariness;
fourth, protecting all dharmas by constantly practicing diligence.
These are the four [practices] by which one reaches the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are four pure practices by which one reaches the site of enlightenment:
the first is the purity of guarding the precepts;
Second is the purity of the nature of the mind;
third is the purity of wisdom;
fourth is the purity of that which is produced.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four further dharmas that disciples and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain:
first, their practice transcends the four dhyānas;
Second, their minds enter into many realms;
third, they practice great compassion toward all sentient beings;
fourth, their eloquence consists of various kinds of voices.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four modes of conduct:
first, delighting in dwelling in seclusion and remaining far removed from the clamor of crowds;
The second is to go forth to those [beings] and practice loving-kindness toward sentient beings;
the third is to be free from flattery, deceit, and evil conduct, and to have no place of attachment;
the fourth is to seek the practice of the Path.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four things that are unimpeded regarding what is asked and cannot be interrupted:
first, not begrudging one's own body or life;
Second, the mind is always joyful;
third, abandoning arrogance;
fourth, constantly practicing and upholding the Dharma.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one’s conduct becomes complete:
first, always knowing the proper seasons and times;
The second is to manifest teachings according to what others prefer;
the third is to always maintain a sense of shame and modesty;
the fourth is to know contentment and moderation.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one’s mental conduct is impartial:
first, to provide respectful instruction according to what is appropriate for each person;
Second, that which is to be taught by the great wisdom of one's vows;
third, not speaking of the long and short [faults] of others;
fourth, when seeing those who speak of faults, approaching them with a heart of loving-kindness and harboring no resentment.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four matters by which one’s name and virtue become fully perfected such that they are not unknown to anyone:
first, to study profound wisdom oneself and simultaneously teach it to others;
Second, when anyone comes to inquire about matters, one completely dispels their doubts;
third, one constantly protects the True Dharma;
fourth, the power of the Buddha’s intent is inexhaustible.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which extensive learning becomes firm and strong:
first, upon hearing the Dharma, one understands where it leads."
Second, not coveting domestic life or dwelling in attachment despite the joy of hearing the Dharma;
third, having heard it, widely proclaiming it and explaining it for all people;
fourth, having heard it, giving rise to the explanations of the noble ones and turning toward the Buddha-way and its teachings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which the teaching of the Dharma and one's reputation and virtue circulate:
first, having first attended to the needs of the assembly, one accepts food as sustenance for protection.
Second, obtaining gains, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, thereby subduing the power of Māra;
third, delighting in the Dharma day and night, being protected by the devas;
fourth, not harassing others.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one illuminates the assembly and attains mastery over the body:
the first is to have few desires.
Second, knowing contentment;
third, being subtle and gentle;
fourth, personally upholding the Dharma.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains the benefit of clear wisdom and preaches the Dharma without deviation:
first, to rescue and deliver others from the fear of birth and death;
Second, not seeking the benefits of worldly offerings;
third, constantly protecting others;
fourth, always abiding in the aspiration for the Path.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one recognizes and repays kindness and understands the consequences of good and evil:
first, to exhort and transform others so that they resolve to attain the Way;
Second, not losing the merit established;
third, self-respectfully recollecting and welcoming future compassion;
fourth, constantly visiting true persons and Dharma masters.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four things that do not destroy loving-kindness:
first, being fully endowed with the power of patience;
Second, not to seduce or disturb the retinues of others;
third, not to abandon great compassion;
fourth, to seek liberation from the causes and conditions of both sin and merit, with one's resolve fixed upon the Path.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four matters for practicing loving-kindness: first, always harmonizing with others;
[the second is... [the third is... [the fourth is... These are the four.
Second, their nature and conduct are gentle and compliant;
third, their practice is fully perfected;
fourth, they gradually draw near to the Way.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one knows an evil teacher:
first, teaching people the lesser path;
The second is to teach others to destroy the resolve of Bodhisattvas;
the third is to teach them to seek fame and reputation, thereby increasing unwholesome dharmas;
the fourth is to teach them to distance themselves from meritorious and wholesome dharmas.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one associates with the World-Honored Ones and all Buddhas:
the first is to always unify the mind.
Second, constantly proclaiming the merits of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
third, upholding the pure precepts;
fourth, maintaining a resolute nature that does not abandon one's original vows.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one’s virtuous conduct is commensurate with making offerings to Bodhisattvas and the Honored Tathāgatas without weariness:
the first is that the Buddhas whom one makes offerings to are the most honored among the Benefactors of the Multitude;
Second, those who see me shall likewise emulate my conduct;
third, upon seeing the Tathāgata, their resolve for the Way shall become firm and steadfast;
fourth, they shall behold the thirty-two marks of a great man, which are the foundation of merit, thereby perfecting their skillful means.
These are the four.

Furthermore, there are four matters by which one contemplates the meaning of the sutras and studies the bodhisattva precepts and practices to attain the most supreme state: the first is to transcend the evil realms;
[the second is... [the third is... [the fourth is... to attain the most supreme state.
Second, constantly exhorting others to establish themselves in the path of goodness;
third, revering the Tathāgata;
fourth, fulfilling one's vows.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters of training:
first, not abandoning the resolve for enlightenment;
The second is equality toward all;
the third is seeking the *pāramitā*;
the fourth is protecting the teachings of the countless Buddhas so that they are not severed.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for practicing pure precepts:
the first is to carry out few affairs;
The second is to understand and realize the practice of emptiness;
the third is not to commit the error of false views or doubt;
the fourth is to be free from a mind of hesitation.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters concerning the lineage of samādhi:
first, not practicing the local dialects of a land; [and so forth].
Second is a mind that is pure and unattached;
third is the accomplishment of the roots of merit;
fourth is drawing slightly near to the Buddha-way.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters that should correspond to pure conduct:
first, to give rise to all roots of goodness;
Second, his mind is tranquil and still, and his conduct is free from attachment;
third, his perceptions accord with the gates of liberation;
fourth, he is serene and settled in the meaning of the Path.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four matters for casting off the defiled mind:
first, to constantly focus one's practice with fear and dread of birth and death;..."
Second, the desire to seek the root of the merit of liberation;
third, to establish nothing within tranquility;
fourth, for the mind to have no arising.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for subduing the mind:

first, for the sake of a single person, one shall wander through birth and death for hundreds of thousands of millions of future eons; [the remaining three are as follows:]... [text continues]... These are the four.
Second, to know the thoughts in the minds of all people, and to preach the Dharma according to their original vows in order to sever their worldly afflictions;

third, to completely abandon all unwholesome dharmas, practice all manner of goodness, sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), subdue the armies of Māra, and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path;
fourth, to proclaim one’s voice throughout the trichiliocosm to preach the Dharma for them.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for subduing the enmity of Māra:
first, observing the pure conduct of illusory phenomena;
Second, attaining the patience of the non-arising of phenomena;
third, severing all matters lacking wisdom;
fourth, having already departed from birth and death, one reverently practices correct conduct.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for contemplating the meaning of the sutras:
first, that dharmas arise through causes and conditions and do not arise without a cause;
Second, to establish the profound Dharma while remaining without a self;
third, to contemplate the empty Dharma without anything arising;
fourth, to be naturally without conceptualization, abiding entirely in stillness.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which the mind does not abandon the Bodhisattva-dharma:
first, not abandoning one's original vow; [and so forth].
The second is to endure suffering and affliction;
the third is to not begrudge one's body or life;
the fourth is to not abandon the practice of the four debts of gratitude.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for transforming people through the Dharma:
first, one should preach the Dharma to those who provide clothing and food as an act of giving.
Second, repeatedly exhorting others to remain steadfast;
third, performing deeds that bring about sovereignty and peace;
fourth, establishing the roots of goodness in others.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one may receive the Dharma with settled certainty and embrace it for practice:
first, although one's roots of goodness may be few, one does not harbor thoughts of contempt toward them.
Second, to constantly practice and uphold conduct that brings peace and security;
third, to fulfill the cultivation of goodness through generosity and the taming of the mind;
fourth, to uphold the meaning of the sutras so that all beings may find refuge in peace and security.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one enters the practice of the Path:
the first is to attain supernormal powers;
Second, to achieve right wisdom;
third, to abide in the mind of the Great Way and penetrate deeply into the immeasurable;
fourth, to ensure that all actions performed are merely the practice of emptiness, without attachment even to liberation.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for cultivating and practicing a mind of loving-kindness:
first, to rescue and protect those who are like illusory transformations;
Second, constantly guiding others to uphold the Dharma;
third, delivering those who are deluded by illusions;
fourth, enabling them to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for cultivating a mind of compassion:
first, to act as a friend to those in the evil realms, so that they may enter the Path, thereby giving rise to compassion for them.
Second, to cause others to leave behind evil transgressions by teaching them to cultivate goodness;
third, to teach those who seek the Lesser Vehicle and exhort them to resolve upon the Great Vehicle;
fourth, when practicing compassion, to embrace that compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for practicing skillful means (upāya-kauśalya):
first, to have the intention directed toward the Way precede all thoughts.
Second, not abandoning the mind of worldly afflictions, much less the mind of skillful means;
third, observing all people and those with various false views as all being vessels for the Dharma;
fourth, seeing all phenomena as the Buddha-dharma, naturally attaining supreme perfect enlightenment, and through the practice of various samādhis, achieving excellent liberation.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
first, constantly disparaging one's own body and one's fundamentally pure mind;
Second, the light mind is naturally like an illusion;
third, all that is done consists solely of the establishment of dharmas;
fourth, the mind is tranquil and unified, free from confusion and distraction.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one can discern the phrases of the Dharma:
first, to cultivate the meaning of wisdom through mindfulness without seeking outward adornment;
The second is to seek only the Dharma and not the person, giving rise to nothing that need be extinguished;
the third is to know that all things are inexhaustible and cannot be exhausted;
the fourth is that what is spoken is unattached and unbound by words and letters.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains dhāraṇī:
first, never being weary of extensive learning and always honoring the Dharma masters;
Second, to constantly practice diligence in preaching the sutras for others;
third, to understand all dharma-words closely without losing their meaning;
fourth, to further cause others to enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata.

These are the four. Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti): first, to deliver those who have not yet been delivered; [the second is to liberate those who have not yet been liberated; the third is to console those who have not yet been consoled; and the fourth is to cause those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa].
The second is to liberate those who have not yet been liberated;
the third is to delight in all dharmas;
the fourth is to never cease virtuous conduct.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains eloquence:
first, when seeing another Dharma teacher’s exposition, not seeking out their faults;
Second, to listen to and gather the meaning of the Dharma without arrogance;
third, not to praise oneself;
fourth, upon seeing those of little wisdom who have not yet studied, not to treat them with contempt or ease.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters through which one practices non-retrogression:
first, not retreating from desire, anger, and ignorance;
Second, not regressing from the conduct of sentient beings;
third, not regressing from all unwholesome dharmas;
fourth, not regressing from the understanding of supreme perfect enlightenment.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters for understanding profound meaning:
the first is to comprehend the twelve links of dependent origination.
Second, naturally attaining the realization of the Buddha-way as the awakening to the true reality;
third, that all dharmas have a single meaning, and that this meaning is entirely empty;
fourth, fully understanding the Buddha-way.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one fulfills their aspirations:
first, the purity of ethical discipline and patience;
The second is to purify and eliminate the evil realms;
the third is to be simple and honest, free from flattery and deceit;
the fourth is to employ skillful means according to one's fundamental practice.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one attains the non-retrogressive dharma of the various pāramitās:
first, to cause each single pāramitā to fully enter into all the pāramitās;
The second is: through skillful means, causing all people to enter [the path], yet there are no such people;
the third is: seeing all dharmas as being entirely one dharma, free from all desires;
the fourth is: seeing all Buddhas as being entirely one Buddha, because of the Dharma-body.
"These are the four [factors] by which one attains the non-retrogressive dharma of the various *pāramitās*.

When the Buddha spoke these four phrases, the illusory man Renxian attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*; filled with joy and exultation, he rose into the air to a height of four zhang and nine chi above the ground.
At that time, the Buddha, seeing what was in the mind of the illusory practitioner Renxian, smiled.
The Venerable Ānanda praised the Buddha with a verse and asked:
“Your extraordinary and immeasurable majesty, Your wisdom surpasses the sun and moon;”
The names of all [Buddhas] throughout the three periods of time are heard; their virtue and renown constitute the *pāramitā* of Fame.
Their knowledge has mastered the three types of perfect penetration, and the Buddha has attained sovereign mastery.
For what reason does the Buddha now smile?
I only pray that you will explain this for me:
how all classes of sentient beings abide and what they rely upon;
how you, O Honored One among Men, have already perceived the minds of all people while remaining free from attachment.
Regarding those of lower, middling, and superior [faculties], may they all be thus purified;
we pray that you now explain the reason for the Buddha’s smile!
When the devas hear this sound, the *gandharvas* likewise do so.
Śakra, the asuras, gandharvas, mahoragas, and even the Brahmā heavens are likewise; their voices are tranquil and pure.
All those various sounds Are ultimately not equal to the Buddha’s.
The light emitted by the moon, And that of the sun and maṇi jewels,
The radiance of Śakra, And all lights including that of Brahmā—
Their light is entirely eclipsed and extinguished, coming to an end so as not to appear again;
yet when the Buddha emits his radiance, it illuminates all the buddha-fields.
Having already realized all profound dharmas, he remains tranquil, empty, and quiescent.
Therein is no self, nor is there a life-span; it is neither existent nor non-existent, for both of these conditions have been eliminated.
The Honored One brings auspiciousness to all the world, moving through it like the light of the moon.
In this world, merely by generating the aspiration and resolving to follow the sublime path—
who today shall abide securely in the Buddha-way and the True Dharma?
Thus, having obtained this body, I take refuge in the Honored One, the Jewel of the Buddha.
Excellent! We pray that you will explain the meaning of your smile today.
The Buddha’s teaching is pure in meaning; for the sake of his disciples, the Honored Buddha has brought peace and security, and his radiance shines like the sun upon all.
For the sake of those of other paths, he taught the meaning of the Pratyekabuddhas;
but for those who seek Buddhahood, he resolved them toward the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
With total retention and freedom from doubt, [he spoke thus] to the God among Gods.
"I only pray that you will explain for me the Buddha-way that ought to be attained.
These flames of the Buddha’s light, pure and extinguishing all defilement,
returned to circle the Buddha’s body and vanished into the crown of his head, no longer visible.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Do you see the illusory man Renxian leaping up into the void? He replied:
“I have already seen the World-Honored One! The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
O son of noble family, O benevolent and virtuous one!

Ninety-two thousand kalpas hence, you shall attain Buddhahood, known as King of Adorned Purity (Śuddhābhirāja) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
The world is named Great Purity, and the eon is called Illusionary Transformation.

In that world of Great Purity of the Tathāgata King of Adornment and Purity, the population is vast, and they dwell in peace, security, and happiness. The five grains are abundant and inexpensive; the land is level and expansive, free of mounds or ruins. It is illuminated by the light of the sun and moon, adorned with various kinds of trees, and fully endowed with manifold fragrances, with banners and streamers constantly suspended.

The people of that land, according to their wishes, all behold the Buddha-land as adorned and pure; everything there is spontaneous, like the palaces made of the seven treasures in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The people of that land all perceive their country as peaceful and elegant; those born in that Buddha-land all seek the supreme vow and are intent upon the Mahāyāna.
The Tathāgata King Adorned and Purified dwells in the world for ten thousand years, and after his parinirvāṇa, the practice of the Dharma shall remain for one hundred million years.
As the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, there was a bodhisattva named Śrutasaṃbhava, to whom the Buddha granted this prediction:

"After my parinirvāṇa, this bodhisattva Śrutasaṃbhava shall attain Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat, named Viśvaprāpta."
At that time, the noble son Bhadrapāla descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha is my teacher; he guides me along the path of goodness.”
"O World-Honored One!
I, together with countless billions of hundreds of thousands of people, take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.

If the Tathāgata is fundamentally non-existent, and the fundamental non-existence of all Buddhas is no different from this, then that which is suchness is indestructible; suchness is immovable, suchness is without conceptualization, suchness is without arising, suchness is without activity, and suchness is without duality. The fundamental non-existence of the Tathāgata is likewise so!"
"I have attained accomplishment because of this.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda asked the noble son Renxian:
"What has been attained within the Dharma of the Tathāgata that you speak of the Tathāgata as being originally non-existent?"
"Now, you have distanced yourself from the original state of non-action? He replied,
"When all dharmas are abandoned and left behind, only then does the Dharma of the Tathāgata arise."
What do you think, Ānanda?

The Tathāgata has fully realized that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*) and thereby attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). For this reason, the Tathāgata’s fundamental non-existence is indestructible; I have likewise attained it, and all people shall also reach this fundamental non-existence.
"What do you think, worthy one?
Is there a duality in the Dharma of the Tathāgata?
"Certainly not, Ānanda!"
The Dharma is neither dual nor non-dual; yet for those who harbor conceptions, their consciousness appears as manifold.
Why is this? Because it is by relinquishing all conceptions that one attains the wisdom of a Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One!
Will this son of good family, Renxian, ever again employ his original illusory transformations to delude the devas and humans?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“In this regard, Renxian has entered the illusion of the wisdom of the Dharma. Why is this so?
"This is because of his use of clear wisdom and eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the noble son Renxian:
"Are you able to transform either the various devas or the people of the world?"
He replied: "Indeed!
Just as you have been transformed by the Buddha's skillful means, so too am I."

Why is this so? To understand non-self is the Great Practice; it is called "having a person" while being without a life-span, and it is said that "there is a person" when there is no person. The Tathāgata has no name and does not abide in the place of enlightenment.
In what dharma is there going and ceasing, such that one speaks of dharmas having coming and going?
How can the teaching-dharma be without parinirvāṇa yet manifest the dharma of nirvāṇa?

For this reason, the World-Honored One speaks of the practice of equanimity, whereby he is able to transform and guide the deluded devas and people of the world, preaching for them the equality of the Tathāgata’s merits.
At that time, the Buddha praised the clansman Renxian:
"Excellent, excellent, Renxian!
Just as you have said, for the sake of those who are greatly deluded, you have preached the Dharma of soundlessness."
At that time, Renxian requested to leave the household life under the Buddha.
The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"You must shave the hair and beard of this illusory man and cause him to become a śramaṇa."
Maitreya received the instruction and immediately had Renxian (Bhadra) go forth into homelessness.
Having fulfilled his intent, he returned and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
This is neither the physical form nor the appearance of a bodhisattva, nor is it that of a śramaṇa. Why is this so?
When a bodhisattva has perfected the various supernormal knowledges and dwells within the triple world to transform and teach all living beings, this constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
When these words were spoken, five thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and two hundred bhikṣus attained liberation through the exhaustion of outflows.
At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named, and how should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'Bestowing the Prediction upon the Illusionist Viśvantara,' and it is also titled 'Gradually Entering the Path to Buddhahood.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

“Ānanda! Any bodhisattva who wishes to see the Buddha for the sake of all beings should receive this sutra, uphold it, recite it, and read it; they should broaden their resolve and explain it to others.”

Why is this so? Because when bodhisattvas seek the Way within these teachings, it constitutes the Dharma of the Mahāyāna Sūtra on Equality; for this reason, this sūtra is titled "Gradually Entering the Meaning of the Way."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“I entrust this sutra to you; keep it in mind and recite it aloud, uphold its scrolls, and if you hear it and practice accordingly, all evils will turn back. You should know that such a person has previously seen five hundred Buddhas before attaining the Way of the Buddha.”
At that time, the son of noble family Renxian addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Those who receive this sutra all possess fundamental merit.
It is so, World-Honored One!”
I too originally studied this.
Why is that? Because those who hear this sutra all possess past roots of goodness and skillful means; my mind is likewise!

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the noble son Renxian, the venerable bhikṣu Ānanda, and the entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, and the people of the world—rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they bowed their heads in prostration and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Illusionist Viśvantara Spoken by the Buddha
